meta.titre: Fruit and Seed Dispersal: agents, adaptations and how to describe them
meta.sous_theme: Methods of dispersal and the features of fruits and seeds that suit them

sections.contenu_markdown:
Under a big mango tree in a compound, dozens of tiny seedlings push up in one crowded patch. Most will die because they share the same shade, water and soil. The plants that spread successfully send their seeds far from the parent.
At the GCE you are asked to define dispersal and to say how a named fruit or seed is suited to its method. Marks go to the pair 'feature plus how it helps', so you need to learn both halves.

items: After fertilisation the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
Seeds need water, oxygen and warmth to germinate.
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### What is dispersal and why does it matter?
**Seed dispersal** is the scattering of seeds or fruits away from the parent plant. Dispersal matters because it:
- reduces competition for light, water and mineral salts between the parent and its seedlings, and among the seedlings themselves;
- lets the species colonise new areas;
- reduces the spread of diseases and pests that attack a crowded group of plants.

Do not confuse dispersal with pollination (the transfer of pollen) or with germination (the growth of the seed into a seedling).

### Agents of dispersal
| Agent | Features of the fruit or seed | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Wind | Light; has a wing, a parachute of hairs or silky fibres that give a large surface area | Dandelion, cotton seed, kapok (silk-cotton) seed |
| Animals, outside the body | Hooks, spines or a sticky surface that cling to fur, feathers or clothes | Hooked fruits of Bidens (blackjack) |
| Animals, inside the body | Fleshy, sweet, often brightly coloured fruit that is eaten; seeds have a hard coat and pass through the gut unharmed, or are dropped away from the tree | Guava, mango, pawpaw |
| Water | Buoyant, with a waterproof husk that holds air | Coconut |
| The plant itself (explosive) | The dry fruit dries out and tension builds in its wall until it splits suddenly and throws the seeds | Pods of many legumes |

### Writing a good answer
Name the agent, state the feature, then say how the feature helps. For example: 'The seed has a tuft of hairs, which gives a large surface area, so the wind can carry it far from the parent.'

variantes.nom: Questions that ask how a named fruit is adapted
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives the name of a fruit or seed and asks about its adaptation
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use three short steps: (1) name the agent, (2) describe the feature that matches it, (3) explain how the feature helps. If you do not know a plant, look at the description given in the question and decide which agent the structure suits: wings and hairs mean wind, hooks mean animal fur, fleshy flesh means animals that eat it, a floating husk means water, a dry pod means explosive splitting.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a practical question asks you to compare how far fruits are carried
variantes.contenu_markdown: Drop several fruits of each kind from the same height and time how long each takes to reach the ground. Repeat each fruit several times and find the mean time. A fruit that falls slowly stays in the air longer, so a wind would carry it farther. Keep the height and the air conditions the same for every fruit, so that the test is fair.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A student collects three fruits: one with many small hooks, one soft, red and sweet, and one with a ring of fine silky hairs.

(a) State the likely method of dispersal of each fruit.
(b) Explain how each fruit is suited to its method.

etapes.justification: 'State' needs short answers, while 'explain' needs a feature and its function.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Three fruits; for each, a method and an explanation.

etapes.action: Match the hooked fruit to its agent.
etapes.justification: Hooks can grip fur or clothes.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Animals, outside the body. The hooks cling to the fur of passing animals and are carried away before dropping off.

etapes.action: Match the soft, red and sweet fruit.
etapes.justification: Colour, softness and sweetness attract animals that eat it.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Animals, inside the body. Animals eat the fruit; the seeds, protected by a hard coat, pass out in the faeces far from the parent plant.

etapes.action: Match the fruit with silky hairs.
etapes.justification: Hairs increase the surface area while the mass stays small.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Wind. The hairs act like a parachute so that the wind carries the light fruit far from the parent.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Hooked fruit: animal dispersal on the outside of the animal, hooks cling to fur. Soft, red, sweet fruit: animal dispersal after eating, hard-coated seeds pass out unharmed. Fruit with silky hairs: wind dispersal, hairs give a large surface area and the fruit is light.

items.erreur_markdown: Seed dispersal is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma.
items.pourquoi_faux: This describes pollination. Dispersal concerns the movement of seeds or fruits away from the parent plant.
items.correction_markdown: Seed dispersal is the scattering of seeds or fruits away from the parent plant.

items.erreur_markdown: Wind-dispersed seeds are heavy so that they fall a long way from the plant.
items.pourquoi_faux: Wind carries light structures. A heavy seed would drop close to the parent.
items.correction_markdown: Wind-dispersed fruits and seeds are light and have wings, hairs or a parachute giving a large surface area.

items.pourquoi_faux: Dispersal only moves the seeds. Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
items.correction_markdown: Dispersal carries seeds away; germination starts later when the conditions are right.

items.erreur_markdown: All fruits dispersed by animals are sweet and juicy.
items.pourquoi_faux: Fruits with hooks or spines are dry and are carried on the outside of the animal.
items.correction_markdown: Animals disperse fleshy fruits that are eaten and dry hooked fruits that cling to fur.

items.enonce_markdown:
Name the most likely agent of dispersal for each fruit or seed.

(a) A very light seed with a tuft of silky hairs.
(b) A fruit covered with hooks.
(c) A fruit with a fibrous, waterproof husk that holds air.
(d) A red, sweet, fleshy fruit.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Wind**.
(b) **Animals** (carried on the outside, on fur or clothes).
(c) **Water**.
(d) **Animals** (they eat the fruit and drop or pass the seeds away from the plant).

items.enonce_markdown: A farmer finds that a large number of seedlings of one tree are growing in a tight group under the parent tree. Give three reasons why this is a disadvantage to the seedlings.
items.solution_markdown:
Award a mark for each of three points.
1. The seedlings compete with each other and with the parent for light, because the parent casts a deep shade.
2. They compete for water and mineral salts in the same patch of soil.
3. Diseases and pests spread easily in a crowded group, and the species cannot spread to new areas.
**Competition (for light, water and minerals) and the spread of disease are the disadvantages.**

items.enonce_markdown:
A student drops three fruits of type A and three fruits of type B from a height of 2 m and records the time of fall of each, in seconds:
type A: 1.2, 1.1, 1.3; type B: 3.4, 3.6, 3.5.

(a) Calculate the mean time of fall for each type.
(b) Which type is more likely to be dispersed by wind? Explain.
(c) State two things the student must keep the same to make the test fair.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) A: $(1.2 + 1.1 + 1.3) \div 3 =$ **1.2 s**. B: $(3.4 + 3.6 + 3.5) \div 3 =$ **3.5 s**.
(b) **Type B**. It falls more slowly, so it stays in the air longer and a wind would carry it farther. This suggests a large surface area for its mass, such as wings or hairs.
(c) The height of the drop and the air conditions (no draught from a fan or window), or the same way of releasing the fruits.

items_markdown: Seed dispersal is the scattering of seeds or fruits away from the parent plant.
Dispersal reduces competition for light, water and minerals, helps the species spread to new areas and reduces the spread of disease.
Wind: light, with wings, hairs or a parachute. Animals: hooks or edible fleshy fruits. Water: buoyant, waterproof husk. Explosive: dry pods that split and throw seeds.
Answer in the order agent, feature, how the feature helps.
Do not confuse dispersal with pollination or germination.
